e.etymology: The name of Geralt of Rivia, hero of Andrzej Sapkowski's Witcher novels, the video games and the Netflix series. It echoes Gerald, a Germanic name meaning rule of the spear.
namesakes: Geralt of Rivia (monster hunter of The Witcher books, games and Netflix series)

assoc.t: Geralt of Rivia, monster-hunting hero of The Witcher

e.etymology: A Sanskrit name from the root radh, to worship or please, the same root as Radha, the beloved of Krishna, and Aradhya.

e.meaning: the firebird reborn from its ashes
e.etymology: A respelling of Phoenix, the bird of Greek and Egyptian legend that burns and rises again from its ashes. This spelling is that of the hero of the 2020 video game Immortals Fenyx Rising.
A clipped spelling of Seven, the number used as a given name, valued for its long association with luck and completeness.
A modern American coinage that joins Ty- to the -lani ending of Leilani and Kehlani; lani is Hawaiian for sky or heaven.
A modern coinage that follows the sound of Versailles, the French royal palace outside Paris.
A respelling of Kaizen, the Japanese word for improvement, known in English as a philosophy of steady, continuous improvement. It is an American choice, not a traditional Japanese given name.
A feminine form of Shawn, the English spelling of Irish Sean, which came through Norman French Jehan from the Hebrew name behind John.
An old phonetic spelling of Samuel, from Hebrew Shemu'el, read as name of God or God has heard. Samuel was the prophet who anointed Saul and David.
From an English surname and place name brought from Normandy, Old French riche mont, splendid hill. The Yorkshire town gave its name to Richmond, Virginia, and many other places.
From an English surname taken from the town of Stafford, Old English for a river crossing beside a landing place.

assoc.t: Matthew Stafford, Super Bowl-winning NFL quarterback

e.etymology: The Spanish, Italian and Portuguese form of Celestine, from Late Latin Caelestinus, from caelestis, heavenly. Five popes took the name.
From Germanic hild, battle, and gard, enclosure. It is best known from Saint Hildegard of Bingen, the 12th-century abbess, composer and visionary, and reached English in the 19th century.
namesakes: Hildegard of Bingen (12th-century German abbess, composer and saint)

e.etymology: A variant of Naomi, close to Noemi, the Latin form used in Spanish and Italian. From Hebrew No'omi, my pleasantness; in the Bible Naomi is the mother-in-law of Ruth.
The Spanish and Polish form of Seraphin, from Latin Seraphinus, from the seraphim, the six-winged angels of Isaiah's vision. The Hebrew word means burning ones.
Probably from Annushka, the Russian pet form of Anna, grace, or from Persian anusha. It became a popular girls' name in India, where it is often treated as Sanskrit.
The English word, from Latin memoria, used as a given name. It is rare in the US and well established in southern Africa, especially Zimbabwe and Malawi.
A respelling of Jordan, from the Jordan River, in Hebrew Yarden, from a verb meaning to descend or flow down. Crusaders brought the name home with water from the river for baptisms.
Mora is the Spanish word for blackberry or mulberry and a common Spanish surname. The 19th-century American name is of unclear source and may be a variant of Maura or Moira.
The Italian form of Latin Camillus, a Roman family name that matched the word for a noble youth who assisted at religious rites.
The Danish and Norwegian form of Michael, from Hebrew Mikha'el, a question meaning who is like God? Michael is the archangel who leads the armies of heaven.
As a Vietnamese girls' name, Diem means beautiful or radiant. In American use it also recalls Latin diem, day, from the phrase carpe diem, seize the day.

assoc.t: Latin for day, as in carpe diem

e.etymology: Anna and Grace written as one name. Anna comes from Hebrew Hannah, favor or grace, and Grace from Latin gratia, so both halves carry the same meaning.
From Hebrew nadav, generous or noble, one who gives freely. In the Bible Nadab is the eldest son of Aaron; Nadav is the modern Israeli form.
An American coinage of the 2000s in the Aiden, Brayden and Jayden family, close to the English surname Bladen.
From Persian mirza, a title for a prince or learned man, formed from mir, commander (Arabic amir), and the ending -zad, born of. A given name in Bosnia and South Asia.
A modern American elaboration of Sky or Skye with the -leigh ending, close in sound to Kylie and Skylar.
A spelling of Arlyn, a 20th-century American name related to Arlene and Arlen, whose own source is uncertain.
A modern American elaboration of Mia or Mya with the -ana ending.
A form of Emmeline, the medieval English version of Old French Ameline, built on the Germanic element amal, work, which also lies behind Amelia.
